title: Age, size and inertia
text:
Age and size: hindering business model renewal
Liability of age and tradition: 
- Large firms are usually inert, oriented towards strengthening their existing   
competences and risking cannibalization of existing products/services.
- Smaller firms are able to adapt faster and generally have shorter communication   
lines and more space for creativity.
The larger firms become, the sooner they are inclined to replicate their business model.
Some solutions (examples from large Dutch banks ABN Amro, ING and Rabobank): 
 collaboration with (fintech) startups and other small firms
 introduction of an innovation centre/studio
 more emphasis on agile methods, responsiveness and intrapreneurship.

title: Industries and markets
text:
Introduction to the concept of corporate scope
 The multi-business company can be conceived of as an assembly of (groups of) business units, each 
of which is responsible for the company’s competitive posture in a distinctive business area.
 The nature of a company’s business areas can be described in terms of either the industries(industry-
oriented approach) or markets (market-oriented approach) in which it has a competitive presence.
 An industry is a group of firms producing similar products and competing for 
the same resources and customers in the marketplace.
 A product market consists of products (goods or services) with similar 
characteristics in terms of features, performance, intended use, and price.
 A geographical market is a distinct geographical area in which products are 
sold and in which the conditions of competition are relatively homogeneous.

title: Internationalization as state and action
text:
Internationalization in a corporate-level strategic context
In a corporate strategy context, the term 
‘internationalization’ typically can have two meanings:
1. The level to which a firm participates in geographical 
markets outside its home market (i.e., how does its 
current geographic scope look like?) 
 the state of internationalization
2. The growth strategy of geographic expansion across 
national borders
 the act of internationalization

title: CAGE and market selection
text:
Geographical market selection (growth)
 One way to decide which country and location to select is by evaluating a firm’s compatibility
with different countries/locations in terms of how ‘distant’ or different they are from a firm’s 
current market(s) in terms of the “CAGE factors”: Cultural, Administrative, Geographical and 
Economic factors.
 Differences between locations can offer opportunities for internationalization as well.
 Other important criteria (besides compatibility and differences) may include market size, 
income level, economic instability, corruption, difficulties to protect IP , security risks, 
sovereign risks, competitive rivalry, etc.

title: Risks, foreignness and outsidership
text:
Risks and costs of internationalization (growth) 
 Establishing operations in a new country implies a larger range of political, economic, legal 
and other macro-environmental factors that have to be dealt with.
 Firms may face economic instability, corruption, security risks, difficulties to protect 
intellectual capital, sovereign risks, and the effects of economic sanctions.
 Liability of foreignness: multinational firms initially face additional costs relative to their 
indigenous competitors when they operate in foreign countries (e.g., adaptation costs, 
discrimination costs, governance costs, appropriation costs).
 Liability of outsidership: additional costs due to not yet having a relevant network position, 
which requires the building of trust and commitment with others.

title: Five entry modes
text:
Modes of internationalization (growth) 
Different entry modes correspond to different levels of associated risks, resource commitment, 
organizational control, and entry speed. Five key entry mode types: 
 Exporting: selling a product produced in a firm’shome country to a foreign country.
 Licensing: licensing agreement with a partner firm located abroad.
 Joint venture: establishing a jointly owned entity with one or more other firms.
 Greenfield investment: constructing a wholly owned subsidiary unit in another country 
from scratch. 
 Brownfield investment: purchasing or leasing of a pre-existing firm or facility in another 
country, or the acquisition of a controlling stake in such a firm or facility.

title: Reasons for internationalization
text:
Reasons for internationalization (growth) 
 A firm’s goals can no longer be met within its current geographical scope.
 Opportunities in another country that promise a higher return on capital.
 Possibilities for achieving economies of scale.
 Distributing risks across different geographical markets.
 Stabilizing earnings and reducing uncertainty about cash low.
 Follow customers (in a B2B market) when these decide to internationalize.
 Tapping into strategically relevant knowledge sources located in another country.
 (…)

title: Intensity, spread and concentration
text:
Levels of internationalization
Dimensions to take into account when assessing a firm’s level of internationalization:
• Intensity of internationalization: the extent to which activities take place away from 
its home country (i.e., the proportion of revenues attributable to ‘foreign’).
• Geographical spread: the spread of foreign activities in terms of the number of 
countries in which they take place.
• Geographic concentration: the degree to which these activities are spatially 
(typically by nation-state) concentrated within specific regions.
Source: Ietto-Gillies (2010)

title: Internationalization and performance
text:
Internationalization levels and performance
 Most studies report an inverted U-shape type of relationship between the level of 
internationalization and corporate performance (in terms of rate of return).
 High levels of internationalization enable firms to benefit more from economies of scale and 
from locational advantages that are present around the globe, however this also comes with 
increased coordination complexity that may become more costly than these benefits.
Note: Having a diversified portfolio may help firms to do better from internationalization 
because these firms are better equipped to manage internal diversity.

title: Divestiture and scope
text:
 The term divestiture (divestment) can in practice refer to the 
disposal of any asset (e.g., staff, a machine or an IP right), but it 
commonly denotes the disposal of a division or controlling interest 
in a subsidiary organization through a sale, exchange or liquidation.
DIVESTITURE-based reconfiguration
 Divestiture formats: 
- spin-off
- split-off
- sell-off
- liquidation 
 A divestiture that narrows an organization’s scope is often referred 
to as a downscoping divestiture.
 When a divestiture comes with the use of permanent cuts in an 
organization’s resource base (e.g., employee layoffs or the closure 
of a facility) to reduce output while maintaining the corporate 
scope intact, this can be labelled a downscaling divestiture.

title: Divestiture transaction formats
text:
 A spin-off and a split-off both imply that a certain division of the firm is turned into a separate, independently operating firm . The 
corporate parent of the divesting firm distributes the shares in the division that is being divested to existing shareholders. 
 In the case of a spin-off, this allocation of shares is in proportion (or ‘pro rate’) to shareholdings. 
 In the case of a split-off, which is less common, the existing shareholders have to make a choice between owning shares in 
the divesting parent firm or owning shares in the business entity that is being divested. 
Note: The choice for either a spin-off or a split-off is usually followed later in time by selling off the newly created business 
entity, implying a permanent change of ownership.
 A sell-off implies that a parent firm sells a subsidiary unit (or a controlling interest in this unit), in which it retains no ownership, to 
another firm. 
 An equity carve-out implies that a parent firm sells shares of a subsidiary, in which it typically retains considerable ownership, to 
public investors.
 Sell-offs and equity carve-outs have in common that they can generate a cash inflow for the divesting parent firm and that they 
constitute a clear change in the shareholders’ ownership structure. These two characteristics set sell-offs and equity carve-outs 
apart from spin-offs and split-offs.

title: Three corporate-center functions
text:
Chandler (1991: 33) described three basic functions of the corporate 
headquarters of multi-business company DuPont:
 value-creation: determining strategies to maintain and utilize for the 
long-term the firm’s organizational skills, facilities and capital and to 
allocate resources to pursue these strategies.
 administrative (loss prevention): monitoring the performance of the 
operating divisions, to check on the use of the resources allocated, 
and – when necessary – redefine the product lines of the divisions   
so as to continue to use effectively the company’s capabilities.
 external relationship management: handling relations of the enterprise 
as a whole with legislatures and other governmental bodies 
concerning taxes, tariffs and regulation.

text:

managers) against standards as set by the corporate parent.
 Taking action to improve the performance of divisions (e.g., by 
replacing managers, restructuring or selling off divisions).
 Challenging divisions and (co)developing their strategy.
 Coaching and training of human resources in the divisions.
Source: Johnson et al. (2005)

title: Potentially value-adding activities II
text:

 Achieving synergies and encouraging inter-division collaboration.
 Enabling leverage (e.g., by combining the purchasing power of 
multiple divisions).
 Providing capital injections to divisions. 
 Moving executives from division to division (cross-fertilization of 
transferable managerial capabilities).
 Providing expertise not available in smaller divisions (e.g., IT, 
personnel and financial services, estates management).
Source: Johnson et al. (2005)

initiative (“knock-on effects”), e.g. affecting moti-

the erroneous belief that all the skills and know-

Business ecosystems
 A market-based value system implies direct arm’s-length market transactions between 
unrelated buyers and sellers that act independently and in their self-interest.

have a common corporate parent.
 A supplier-mediated value system implies that activities in different stages of a value

 An ecosystem implies interactions among a multilateral set of entities that offer 
complementary products and that, in doing do, contribute to joint value creation.

 Complementarity is when a certain product (i.e., a good or service),

coordination among these entities in specific ways, or without

Equity joint venture (EJV) (either 50/50 or majority/minority)
 (E)JV: two or more organizations establish a separate, jointly owned and independently operating entity that is governed 
by a board of directors in which typically each of these partner organizations is represented. 
 As these organizations allocate their residual rights of control (in proportion to their equity participation) to this board, an 
EJV arrangement reduces their need to specify all contingencies in their initial agreement (this also applies to other types 
of equity alliances).
 An EJV coexists with the organizations that incorporated this entity, which share not only the entity’s ownership and 
governance but also the returns and risks of this entity.
 Profits resulting from the joint venture are allocated in proportion to shareholdings, which sets this type of arrangement 
apart from a cooperative.
 The EJV equity ratio can change over time.
 EJV’s can be operating entities or non-operating entities (or a combination of both):
- non-operating means that the EJV is purely legal and administrative entity that contracts with each of the       
participating partners to perform operational activities

title: Cooperatives
text:
Source: Volberda et al. (2023)
Cooperative (co-op)
 Co-op: organizations collaborate as members of a cooperative that they collectively own and run with the purpose of 
providing services to each of the members (which could also be individual workers or consumers or other cooperatives)
 These members have limited liability and contribute equally to the cooperative’s equity capital, from which they benefit 
in proportion to their ‘patronage’ or transactions with the cooperative – that is, in proportion to their use of the 
cooperative’s good or services.
 Cooperatives operate on a democratic ‘one member, one vote’-principle, meaning control is allocated evenly among 
their members. 
 A cooperative can have many members.
 Types of cooperatives include producer and marketing cooperative (e.g., FrieslandCampina), purchasing cooperatives 
(e.g., Norway’s Salmon Group), credit unions (e.g., Capital Credit Union), retail cooperatives (e.g., Coop Amba), social 
cooperatives (e.g., Gruppo Cooperativo CGM in Italy) and R&D cooperatives (e.g., Covid R&D Alliance).

 Companies taking minority equity positions in other companies are usually granted representation on the board
 A cross-shareholding (equity swap) implies that two or more companies take non-controlling stakes in each other
 A keiretsu refers to a Japanese business structure that is comprised of a set of vertically related companies (vertical 
keiretsu) or horizontally related companies (horizonal keiretsu) that are tied together by cross-shareholdings and

title: Licensing
text:
Licensing agreements
Source: Volberda et al. (2023),
 A licensing agreement between a licensor (the company granting the license) and licensee implies that the latter party is 
authorized to use and earn revenue from certain intellectual property and/or other assets of the licensor in exchange for 
a negotiated payment.
 License payments often consist of an upfront lump-sum fee in conjunction with ongoing, usage-based fees called royalties 
(e.g., €0,50 for each unit sold, or 10% of revenues), but other terms are not uncommon.
 The licensor and licensee may agree on a certain cap on the amount of royalties payable under the life of the agreement 
or in any given specific period. They may also agree on certain scaling terms.
 Cross-licensing agreements (usually royalty-free) imply that two or more companies grant a license to each other, such as 
patents over different aspects of the same technology or product.
 Exclusive licensing agreement versus sole licensing agreement versus non-exclusive licensing agreement.
 Besides stipulating compensation and license exclusivity and duration, licensing agreements typically include provisions 
concerning the field of use of the licensed property (e.g., specifying the range of products that the licensee is allowed to 
sell utilizing this property and the geographical area of these sales), performance guarantees (e.g., quality standards and a 
minimal guaranteed use of the licensed property), license transferability and dispute settlement

title: Franchising
text:
Franchising agreements
Source: Volberda et al. (2023),
 Franchising is a special, comprehensive form of licensing.
 A franchising agreement between a franchisor (granting a franchising license) and a franchisee implies that the latter is 
granted the right to use a certain franchise formula, typically in a specific geographical area, owned by the franchisor. 
 Such a formula typically consists of a combination of intellectual property (including brand identity elements) and 
transferable business practices that enable the franchisee to duplicate a certain business model. 
 Franchisors usually provide ongoing guidance, support and training to their franchisees. 
 Many franchise rights are granted in exchange for an upfront fee and royalties along with fees for goods and services such 
as marketing. 
 Franchisees usually have to abide by a set of rules and core principles as imposed by the franchisor concerning operations 
and marketing. The level of direction and control exerted by the licensor is more significant than with licensing 
agreements that do not involve franchising.
Note: While all franchising agreements are licensing agreements, 
not all licensing agreements include franchising.

title: Reasons for strategic alliances
text:
Choice of alliance partner
 Managing risks and uncertainties (sharing risks)
 Overcoming funding limitations
 Improving economies of scope or scale (lower average-production costs)
 Access to complementary resources such as new technologies
 Access to new markets (e.g., making use of the partner’s market reputation, knowledge of local/regional market, political 
contracts, distributional channels, etc.)
 Strengthening one’s position in the marketplace: leveraging in-house R&D capabilities, ensuring a more reliable supply 
chain, negotiating purchasing discounts, creating a more encompassing value proposition, acquire data, etc.)
 Speeding things up (e.g., new technology or product development, market entry, etc.)
 Other potential reasons: allowing for greater flexibility, enhanced learning, closing of certain skill gaps, generation of 
additional income streams, and more lobbying power.

title: Three partner traits
text:
Choice of alliance partner
 An appropriate alliance partner contributes to the alliance’s intended goals without this being at the expense of the 
company’s other strategic goals.
 At least three different partner traits have a positive effect on alliance performance (Shah & Swaminathan, 2008):
 partner complementarity: the degree to which a partner can contribute valuable nonoverlapping resources and 
capabilities to the alliance (e.g., Dyer & Singh, 1998; Mowery et al., 1996) 
 partner compatibility: the fit between partners in terms of, for instance, corporate culture, type of resources, 
decision-making style and working practices (e.g., Mitsuhashi & Greve, 2017). 
 partner commitment: a partner’s willingness to contribute the resources required to achieve the alliance goals even 
when this requires making minor sacrifices (Gundlach et al., 1995).
 The criticality of these traits in comparison to each other can vary according to conditions such as partners’ size and 
longevity (Rothermael & Boeker, 2008)and the extent to which it is clear to them what exactly should be done 
during the lifetime of the alliance to achieve its long-term goals (Kale & Singh, 2009).

title: Resource quality, trust and coordination risk
text:
Choice of alliance partner (cont.)
Other relevant factors to take into account when choose an alliance partner:
 the quality of the alliance-relevant resources and capabilities owned by companies (Das & Teng, 2000): 
 the perceived risk of opportunistic behavior of a possible alliance partner during the course of the alliance (Castañer 
& Oliveira, 2020; Lioukas & Reuer, 2020)
 Trustworthiness (Ariño & Ring, 2010): goodwill trust (typically at the opposite of opportunism) & competence trust
 Trust enhancing:
 a favorable reputation status or reputationof a company itself (Hubbard et al., 2018; Stern et al., 2014) and of its 
alliance partners (Mukherjee et al., 2013)
 familiarity with a company because of prior alliance ties (Gulati, 1995)
 The ex-ante perceived difficulties and complexities in properly managing or coordinating the relationship with a 
partner throughout the post-formation stage (Castañer & Oliveira, 2020; Das & Teng, 2001; Gulati & Singh, 1998).

title: Coopetition
text:
Coopetition: Partnering up with a competitor
Source: Volberda et al. (2023)
Coopetition often implies that cooperative and competitive interactions take place simultaneously but in…
 … distinct product markets (for example, BMW and Mercedes-Benz cooperating in the mobility services market but 
competing in the market for premium vehicles)
 … distinct geographical markets (for example, probiotic yoghurt drink producers Danone and Yakult cooperating in India 
but competing in Europe)
 … distinct stages of the supply chain (for example, Coca-Cola and Pepsi cooperating to foster post-consumption recycling 
while battling each other in the pre-consumption marketing arena).

title: Post-formation management
text:
Alliance management and dynamics in the post-formation stage 
Source: Volberda et al. (2023)
 The launch of the alliance marks the beginning of its post-formation phase, the duration of which can be undefined
or predetermined. During this phrase, alliance partners engage in a cooperative relationship that is negotiated in a 
continuing communicative process as they contribute towards achieving the goal(s) of their alliance.
 For most types of alliances, the success of alliances once they are up and running is determined for an important part 
by how companies manage the interdependencies, operational complexities and uncertainties that exist and arise in 
these alliances during the post-formation phase. 
 The high alliance failure rate of around 60 to 70 percent (Hughes & Weiss, 2007) indicates that this can be 
challenging.

title: Six changing dimensions of collaboration
text:
Characteristics of interorganizational collaborations that can change over time 
Source: Majchrzak et al. (2015) 64
1. Goal or mission of the collaboration: add new goal, change priority ranking of existing goals, 
or modify, replace or drop a certain goal.
2. Organizational structure: extent of formalization and standardization of roles, procedures and 
processes of interorganizational collaboration.
3. Contract frame: transactional versus relational elements in the interorganizational 
agreements on which collaborating firms rely in their interactions.
4. Interaction style: from competitive to cooperative (higher degree of open information sharing, 
without hidden agendas) and vice versa on a continuum scale.
5. Decision-making control: the locus of interorganizational decision making.
6. Actor composition: adding of new actors (i.e., companies, other organizations or individuals) 
or the exclusion or replacement of existing ones.
